newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen says Krupp bid hurts shareholders.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen says Krupp bid hurts shareholders.

text.p: German industrial group Thyssen AG said on Monday that 25 percent of its shareholders had indicated they would reject a hostile takeover bid by rival Fried. Krupp AG Krupp-Hoesch.

Thyssen, which is negotiating to form a joint steel company with Krupp, also said it could not see how Krupp could afford a debt-financed takeover. It added minority shareholders would suffer from a hostile deal because dividends would be slashed.
Thyssen says Krupp bid hurts shareholders
In contrast, a merger of steel operations would present far fewer financial risks and achieve 75 percent of possible synergy effects between the two firms, Thyssen said.
"The additional high financial risks, which arise completely out of a hostile takeover, bear no relation to the achievable gains," the company said in a statement.

A hostile takeover would leave a highly leveraged company with 62 billion marks in annual sales, 48 billion marks in liabilities -- including 20 billion marks in debt and only three billion marks in shareholder equity, Thyssen said.

"This high financial risk, compounded by the cyclical steel market, cannot be in the interest of shareholders," the company said. "For an internationally active business such a financial structure bears unjustifiable risks for all concerned."

A full takeover would require 13.6 billion marks in debt financing at the cash price of 435 marks a share which has been announced by Krupp, which would have to be repaid within a few years, Thyssen said.
"It is incomprehensible how this sum plus interest can be repaid in the short term through synergies and the sale of business areas," Thyssen said.

Based on its analysis, Thyssen believed Krupp would only seek to buy 60 percent of its shares -- enough to obtain full control of Thyssen's cash reserves and the right to sell off non-steel subsidiaries to pay for the takeover.
"For the remaining minority shareholders of Thyssen, only a minimal dividend is foreseen," Thyssen said, adding this would be a "glaring violation" of the rights of its remaining shareholders.
The two sides are holding talks on a friendly merger of their steel operations. A deadline has been set for this Thursday by Krupp, which will reinstate its hostile bid if no deal is reached.
